Execute a `bash` command. Use this for shell semantics — pipes, env, processes, git, package managers, build/test runners, anything genuinely interactive or multi-step.

**Translate these to a dedicated tool instead:**
- `cat` / `head` / `tail` (known path) → `Read`
- `sed` / `awk` (in-place edit) → `Edit`
- `echo > file` / `cat <<EOF` → `Write`
- `find` / recursive `ls` to locate files by name pattern → `Glob` (plain `ls <known-directory>` is fine for listing a directory)
- `grep` / `rg` (search file contents) → `Grep`
- `echo` / `printf` (talk to the user) → just output text directly

The dedicated tools render in the per-tool permission UI and keep raw stdout out of the conversation; that is why they are worth reaching for whenever one fits.

**Output:**
The stdout and stderr will be combined and returned as a string. The output may be truncated if it is too long. If the command exits non-zero, the output ends with a `Command failed with exit code: N` line; a command killed by its timeout or interrupted by the user ends with its own message instead.

Background execution is disabled for this agent. Do not set `run_in_background=true`.

**Guidelines for safety and security:**
- Each shell tool call will be executed in a fresh shell environment. The shell variables, current working directory changes, and the shell history is not preserved between calls. To run a command in a particular directory, pass the `cwd` argument (or use absolute paths) rather than relying on a `cd` from an earlier call.
- The tool call will return after the command is finished. You shall not use this tool to execute an interactive command or a command that may run forever. For possibly long-running commands, set the `timeout` argument in seconds. The default is 60s; foreground commands allow up to 300s; a foreground command that hits its timeout is killed.
- Avoid using `..` to access files or directories outside of the working directory.
- Avoid modifying files outside of the working directory unless explicitly instructed to do so.
- Never run commands that require superuser privileges unless explicitly instructed to do so.

**Guidelines for efficiency:**
- Use `&&` to chain commands that genuinely depend on each other, e.g. `npm install && npm test`. Independent read-only commands (separate `git show`, `ls`, or status checks) should be issued as separate parallel Bash calls in one response, not chained into a single call — chaining serializes their execution and mixes their output. Do not stitch outputs together with `echo` separators.
- Use `;` to run commands sequentially regardless of success/failure
- Use `||` for conditional execution (run second command only if first fails)
- Use pipe operations (`|`) and redirections (`>`, `>>`) to chain input and output between commands
- Always quote file paths containing spaces with double quotes (e.g., cd "/path with spaces/")
- Compose multi-step logic in a single call with `if` / `case` / `for` / `while` control flows.
- Do not set `run_in_background=true`; background task management tools are not available.

**Commands available:**
The following common command categories are usually available. Availability still depends on the host, so when in doubt run `which <command>` first to confirm a command exists before relying on it.
- Navigation and inspection: `ls`, `pwd`, `cd`, `stat`, `file`, `du`, `df`, `tree`
- File and directory management: `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `mkdir`, `touch`, `ln`, `chmod`, `chown`
- Text and data processing: `wc`, `sort`, `uniq`, `cut`, `tr`, `diff`, `xargs`
- Archives and compression: `tar`, `gzip`, `gunzip`, `zip`, `unzip`
- Networking and transfer: `curl`, `wget`, `ping`, `ssh`, `scp`
- Version control: `git`; for GitHub-hosted work (PRs, issues, CI runs, API queries) prefer the `gh` CLI when installed — it carries the user's GitHub auth and can return structured JSON
- Process and system: `ps`, `kill`, `top`, `env`, `date`, `uname`, `whoami`
- Language and package toolchains: `node`, `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, `python`, `pip` (use whichever the project actually relies on)

tools.description:

If the user provides a concrete file path to a text file, call Read directly. Do not `Glob`, `ls`, or otherwise pre-check known text file paths; missing or invalid file paths return errors you can handle. Do not use Read for directories; use `ls` via Bash for a known directory, or Glob when you need files matching a name pattern (Glob lists files only, never directories). path.description: Path to a text file. Relative paths resolve against the working directory; a path outside the working directory must be absolute. Directories are not supported; use `ls` via Bash for a known directory, or Glob for pattern search.

line_offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Omit to start at line 1. Negative values read from the end of the file; the absolute value cannot exceed 1000.

n_lines.description: The number of lines to read; the tool also applies its internal cap. Omit to read up to the internal cap of 1000 lines.

Probing complete. Here is the behavioral specification.

# DATES highlighter spec (`--enable dates --disable-builtin-keywords`)

## 1. Exact ANSI styling

Every styled element is wrapped individually as `ESC[<code>m … ESC[0m`:

| Element | SGR | cat -v open |
|---|---|---|
| date numbers (year, month, day) | magenta fg 35 | `^[[35m` |
| time numbers (hour, min, sec, fraction digits) | blue fg 34 | `^[[34m` |
| date inner separators `-` `/` | dim 2 | `^[[2m` |
| time inner separators `:` and fraction separator `.` `,` `:` | dim 2 | `^[[2m` |
| date→time separator char (space, tab, `T`, any `\s`) | red fg 31 | `^[[31m` |
| trailing `Z` | red fg 31 | `^[[31m` |

Each number group and each separator char gets its own open/reset pair; there is no nesting. Example — `2022-09-09 07:46:34`:
`^[[35m2022^[[0m^[[2m-^[[0m^[[35m09^[[0m^[[2m-^[[0m^[[35m09^[[0m^[[31m ^[[0m^[[34m07^[[0m^[[2m:^[[0m^[[34m46^[[0m^[[2m:^[[0m^[[34m34^[[0m`

## 2. Match rules (equivalent regexes)

No word boundaries anywhere — matches start/end mid-token, even between digits.

**Date YMD** (all three numbers magenta, both separators dim):
```
(19\d{2}|20\d{2})([-/])(0[1-9]|[12][0-9]|3[01])([-/])(0[1-9]|[12][0-9]|3[01])
```
- Year strictly 1900–2099 (`1899`/`2100` fail; this is why `12345-09-09` doesn't match at offset 1 — `2345` is out of range).
- Month and day use the *same* 01–31 validation — month is NOT limited to 12: `2022-13-13`, `2022-31-31` match; `2022-00-01`, `2022-01-32`, `2022/13/45` don't. No month-length logic (`2022-04-31` matches).
- Exactly 2-digit month/day (`2022-9-9` fails), exactly 4-digit year.
- Separators are independent: mixed `2022-09/09` matches. `.` is NOT a date separator (`2023.10.02` no match).

**Date DMY** — `DD[-/]MM[-/]YYYY` with the same component validations — matches, BUT THE OUTPUT BYTES ARE REORDERED (genuine surprise, verified via `od -c`): input `31/12/2022` is emitted as `2022/31/12`, i.e. `year sep1 day sep2 month` (sep chars keep source order: `31/12-2022` → `2022/31-12`). Styling identical to YMD. A reimplementation must reproduce this reordering byte-for-byte. 2-digit-year forms (`09-09-22`) never match.

**Time** (hour/min/sec/fraction digits blue; `:` and fraction separator dim):
```
([T\s])?([01]?\d|2[0-3])(:)([0-5]\d)(:)([0-5]\d)([.,:]\d*)?(Z)?
```
- Optional leading separator group: exactly ONE char matching `[T\s]` (space, tab, `\v`, `\f`, `\r` all verified red), styled red. It belongs to the time match — it fires after ANY preceding text or at line start (` 07:46:34` → red space; `hello world 07:46:34` → only last space red; `x 25:99:99` → nothing, invalid time kills the whole match). Lowercase `t` does NOT match this group (`2022-09-09t07:46:34`: `t` plain, date and time still match separately). `_` plain too.
- Hour 1–2 digits, 0–23. Because there are no boundaries, invalid hours degrade to substrings: `24:00:00` highlights `4:00:00`; `29:00:00` → `9:00:00`; `107:46:34` → `07:46:34`.
- Minute/second exactly 2 digits, 00–59 (`07:5:00`, `07:60:00`, `07:46:60` fail).
- Fraction: optional, one separator from `[.,:]`, then `\d*` — zero or more digits, unbounded length (30 digits fine). The separator alone still styles dim: `07:46:34.` → trailing `.` dim; `07:46:34.x` → `.` dim, `x` plain. Only one fraction: `07:46:34,5,5` → second `,5` plain.
- Optional trailing uppercase `Z`, red. Lowercase `z` plain. `07:46:34.Z` → `.` dim + `Z` red.

**No other date concepts match**: timezone offsets (`+02:00`, `-0500`) are never styled; am/pm never styled; `HH:MM` without seconds never matches; month/weekday names (`Aug`, `Sun`, `September`, `Monday`) never styled; unix timestamps (`1663776394`) not matched; `Aug 14 2022`, `14 Aug 2022`, `Sep 09, 2022` not matched. The red space in syslog lines like `Aug 14 00:30:00` is purely the time's leading separator group — "Aug 14" is unstyled.

## 3. Boundary/edge examples (input → output, `^[` = ESC)

- `2022-13-45` → unchanged (day 45 > 31)
- `02022-09-09` → `0` + styled `2022-09-09`; `2022-09-090` → styled date + plain `0`
- `(2022-09-09)`, `[07:46:34]`, `é2022-09-09é` → match, punctuation/unicode untouched
- `xT07:46:34` → `x` plain, `T` red, time blue; `TT07:46:34` → first `T` plain, second red
- `07:46:34 08:46:34` → both times blue, middle space red
- `2022-09-09   07:46:34` (3 spaces) → date magenta, 2 plain spaces, 1 red space, time blue
- `2022-09-09 25:99:99` → date magenta, everything after plain (separator only styles with a valid time)
- `07:46:34Zx` / `07:46:34ZZ` → one red `Z`, rest plain
- `12:00:00 AM` / `10:51:19pm` → time blue, am/pm plain
- `31/12/2022 07:46:34` → `2022/31/12` (reordered, magenta/dim) + red space + blue time
- Exit code 0 in all cases.

## 4. Surprises / quirks

1. **DMY reordering** — the emitted byte stream for `DD[-/]MM[-/]YYYY` is `YYYY sep1 DD sep2 MM`. Biggest gotcha for a byte-for-byte reimplementation.
2. Month is validated as 01–31, not 01–12; year is validated as 1900–2099.
3. The red date→time "separator" is really an optional leading `[T\s]` group of the time match, so it fires after arbitrary text, at line start, and even with no date at all.
4. Fraction digits are `\d{0,}` — a trailing bare `.`/`,`/`:` after seconds is styled dim with zero digits following.
5. Case sensitivity is strict: `T`/`Z` uppercase only.
6. No word boundaries: matches happily start/end adjacent to letters, digits, or unicode; invalid leading digits are simply skipped to a valid substring (`24:00:00` → `4:00:00`).
